summary.title: Falsehoods software teams believe about user feedback
summary.one_liner: User feedback is often interpreted differently from how users intended it, and this list of common false assumptions shows where teams misread bug reports and feature complaints.
takeaways: Users rarely share the precision, shared context, or consistent terminology that software teams take for granted.
Phrases like 'X is broken', 'sometimes broken', 'critical bug', and 'urgent' can mean very different things to different users.
Assuming feedback is always literal can lead to over-reacting to minor issues or dismissing serious ones.
Productive feedback relationships build over time as engaged users adopt team terminology and teams learn to assess feedback from users further away, especially internal users and management.
summary.summary: This thoughtbot blog post presents a list of about 40 false assumptions software teams make when reading user feedback, in the style of the "falsehoods programmers believe" genre. Each item pairs a common user statement, such as "X is broken" or "this bug is urgent", with the unwarranted assumption behind it. The author explains that these assumptions stem from teams' own careful, precise communication, which doesn't carry over to ordinary users. The post ends by noting the statements are usually true but not always, so teams should be cautious.
